title: Bodhicitta
hookLine: the mind that wants to wake up for the sake of all beings

lines: PUT ON YOUR OWN MASK FIRST.
ONLY TO HELP THE NEXT PERSON.
cards: Every flight, the same speech. If the cabin loses pressure, put on your own mask first, then help the person next to you. Nobody can help anyone after passing out.
Now take it one step further. Someone puts on their own mask only so they can help the person beside them. And the row behind.
And every passenger on every plane. In Mahayana and Tibetan Buddhism, that is the reason given for walking the path at all.

teach.b: Bodhicitta. Bodhi, awakening, the word you met under the tree. Citta, mind or heart.
The awakening mind: the wish to wake up not just for yourself, but so you can help every being do the same. In Tibetan practice it's the engine of everything.
The four thoughts turn the mind; bodhicitta tells it where to go.

One teacher Tibetans study closely on bodhicitta is Shantideva, an Indian monk. A story people tell: at the monastery of Nalanda, the other monks thought he was lazy, good only for eating, sleeping and strolling around.
To embarrass him, they asked him to teach in public. He sat down and recited a whole long poem, The Way of the Bodhisattva, and the monks were stunned.

teach.h: WANTING TO GO, THEN SETTING OUT.
teach.b: In it he draws a simple line: there's wanting to go on a journey, and there's actually setting out. Bodhicitta has both: the wish, then the steps, in giving, patience, effort and the rest.
Near its close comes a vow people still say today, in paraphrase: for as long as space remains and beings remain, may I remain too, to ease the world's suffering.
Here the traditions differ, so it's worth saying who says what.

In the Theravada, the elders honor the bodhisattva's road as the Buddha's own long path through the Jataka lives, and the usual aim is awakening as an arahant, though some Theravada Buddhists take up the bodhisattva path too.
In the Mahayana and the Vajrayana, bodhicitta is placed at the start of the path for everyone. That's why Tibetan practices end by dedicating whatever good was done to all beings. Not for me.

how: Mahayana and Tibetan Buddhists generate bodhicitta at the start of practice, often reciting a short refuge and bodhicitta verse, and end by dedicating the merit to all beings; many also take formal bodhisattva vows.

o: a sudden flash of awakening in one sit
a bell rung to close a meditation
the wish to wake up for all beings

games.q: match the pieces of the awakening mind.

s: bodhicitta is the wish to wake up for your own sake only
it's the wish to wake up so you can help every being do the same.
Shantideva's fellow monks thought he was lazy
a story people tell: they asked him to teach to embarrass him, and he recited the whole poem.
Shantideva distinguishes wanting to go from actually setting out
bodhicitta has both: the wish and the steps.

games.q: you're Shantideva. the monks of Nalanda, who think you're lazy, have set up a high seat and asked you to teach in public. what do you do?
o: sit down and recite a whole poem on the bodhisattva's way.
games.why: the story says he recited The Way of the Bodhisattva, and the monks were stunned; it's still studied across the Tibetan world.

practice: Before you sit, silently set the intention: whatever good comes from this, may it help someone, and then widen it: may it help everyone. Sit with the breath as usual; you don't need to feel anything special.
At the end, if you'd like, give it away once more: whatever good came from this, for all of us.

wordCard.voice: Bodhicitta. The awakening mind: the wish to wake up for the sake of all beings, and the steps that follow the wish.

orig.note: Sanskrit bodhicitta: bodhi (awakening) + citta (mind, heart). Tibetan: jangchub sem.

carryVoice: Your line: for all of us. The wish, and then the steps. Day three hundred twelve is in the books.

sources.ref: Shantideva, Bodhicaryavatara 1.15–16 (wishing to go and going)
Shantideva, Bodhicaryavatara 10.55 (as long as space remains)
